prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level, enabling frequency comparison and tests of physics at unprecedented precision

statement.case_for: I keep B034 with Katori and Ye as my single-achievement position. The chair asked whether the clocks have produced something nature did not let us guess, and I should answer from the experimental record and not from the instrument's promise. First, the lattice itself turned out to be a many-body system: Ye's group observed density-dependent and spin-exchange interaction shifts between fermions that were expected to be non-interacting, and then used them, which led to clocks operating in a regime where collective quantum effects matter and to SU(N) many-body physics in a clock lattice. Second, gravitational redshift was resolved across a millimetre-scale sample, so a relativistic effect is now measured within a single atomic cloud, which was not possible with any earlier clock. Third, clock-to-clock comparisons across laboratories and fibre links give bounds on variation of fundamental constants and on ultralight dark matter that no other technique matches. These are measurements, not prospects, and the clock is the single instrument that delivers them. On the incremental-precision objection: the comb (2005) gave a ruler for optical frequency, and Wineland's work (2012) gave control of one ion with a limited signal-to-noise ratio. The magic-wavelength lattice is a different concept, because it makes it possible to interrogate very many atoms with the trap perturbation cancelled by design. That change of principle, not just a smaller error bar, is what took stability and uncertainty to 10^-18. Attribution remains compact: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength scheme and demonstrated it with Takamoto, and Ye's group realised the flagship performance and the new physics listed above.
statement.case_against: The weakest points are unchanged and I cannot dismiss them. This is the third prize in a line from Hall and Haensch to Wineland, so a reader might see B034 as a continuation of a precision-measurement tradition. The credit problem is real: Takamoto and Katori's 2005 demonstration, Lemonde's SYRTE work, and Ludlow, Bloom and others at NIST and JILA hold parts of the achievement, and a two-name prize leaves them out. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so some of the practical weight is still to come. I also recognise that my own field makes me comfortable with measurement-first arguments, and that colleagues in condensed matter may judge B046 or B028 to have a larger footprint across physics. In round 1 I have not found a defect in those cases, only a difference in what I weigh most.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B034 with Katori and Ye and flags her own field as a risk of overvaluing the elegance. The chair asked both of us for a concrete finding obtained with lattice clocks.
responses.response: I think we should answer the chair's question together and specifically. The three results I would put on the table are the observation of fermion interaction shifts in the lattice and their use for many-body clock physics, the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, and the constants and dark-matter bounds from comparisons. I would not rest the case on geodesy or the redefinition, which are consequences. We also share a risk, and I would rather have a colleague outside atomic physics test our case than let two members from the same community settle it. On names, I think Katori and Ye is the right slate and I do not support adding a third, because every candidate third name (Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow) weakens the clean story of one concept and one flagship realisation.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes two parts, Halzen alone for IceCube and MacDonald with Jarillo-Herrero for twisted bilayer graphene, and says he would accept B028 if a solo IceCube award cannot be defended.
responses.response: I respect the principle that discoveries come first and that two distinct achievements fit a physics prize. The problem I see is in the allocation. A solo name for a detector built by a large collaboration, with AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal behind it, is the credit weakness you concede yourself, and putting a one-person part next to a two-person part shows the three-seat ceiling pushing the committee into choices made by arithmetic. I would rather have a single part whose names hold without apology. If the committee does go with two parts, I would ask you whether Bistritzer can be added to B046 by dropping the IceCube part, since by your own account that is the bigger gap.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B046 with Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer and would not wait for the pairing mechanism, since the prize is for the discovery.
responses.response: Your change from Andrei to Bistritzer addresses the objection I raised in round 1, and I think the logic of the citation is now consistent: the 2011 prediction credited to both authors and the 2018 experiment credited to its leader. I accept your argument on maturity too. The existence of the correlated phases is reproduced by many groups with different probes, and that is what the Nobel criteria need; the pairing mechanism is an explanation, and prizes have been awarded before it was settled. My remaining concern is Andrei and the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto theory, which three names cannot cover. That is a priority question I cannot settle from memory, but it is the reason B046 stays a strong alternative for me and not my first position.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B028 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp and answers that it extends the 2016 prize without repeating it, while conceding that the HgTe edge conductance fell short of perfect quantisation and that Hasan would be an equally defensible name.
responses.response: Your argument that symmetry-protected band topology in real materials is distinct from the 2016 topological-phase prize is convincing to me, and I would not call B028 a duplicate. As an experimentalist I put more weight on your second concession, though. If the HgTe signal is short of quantisation and the 3D strand with Hasan is the part most reproduced across materials, then the experimental half of the trio is thinner than the theory half, and the committee has to decide whether it prizes the 2D observation or the class of materials. I think the citation has to state that choice. I would be able to support B028 if the committee fixes its scope, which is why it remains my second alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the three concrete clock results I listed (many-body interaction shifts, millimetre redshift, constants and dark-matter bounds) as discoveries and not as precision refinement.

Whether Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom or others have claims strong enough to alter the Katori and Ye slate; my priority recollections are from memory and are not verified against the supplied text.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be waited for; I think the demonstrated performance is sufficient, but I cannot say what colleagues will weigh.
Whether the pairing mechanism and eight-year age of B046, or the credit boundaries of B028, are weaker or stronger than I have assumed, since condensed matter is outside my expertise.
statement.conflict_note: No change in my disclosure. I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Ye is in the JILA lineage of Hall, but I have no direct collaboration with Katori or Ye and see no need to recuse myself on B034, though the committee may decide otherwise. I have no links to the people credited on B046 or B028. My WACQT leadership overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, which bears on B035, which is not in my configuration. Lindroth and I are both from the atomic-physics community and both prefer B034, which I think the committee should weigh when counting support.
